{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-hi-x","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"f527a9daf1d2140ea5f23fc3f545b61ae74a0b729a654c3825b13473979e002a","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-hi-class-3:lineage:59","source_registry_sha256":"1323c0f691f132d6e9e9a263c68306b972b82c8bbaa5a48a33a79177660764be","source_liveness_sha256":"27cf6d56fae2d5323c61bcbb69f0d992aeceb71a7dae4302b1f14baa17651cb0"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Downshifting Cautions, Parking, Turn and Hazard Signals, Traffic Mix and Inclement Weather","heading":"C — Downshifting Cautions, Parking, Turn and Hazard Signals, Traffic Mix and Inclement Weather","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Downshifting Cautions, Parking, Turn and Hazard Signals, Traffic Mix and Inclement Weather

FACT_ID: sec14-F01 | anchor: A01
Most automatic transmissions downshift when the selector is moved to the next lower position, but above about sixty miles per hour they will not, so the vehicle must first slow before an automatic transmission can downshift [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec14-F02 | anchor: A01
Routine downshifting to slow down is not recommended because it decelerates the vehicle sharply without lighting the stop lamps to warn following drivers, so downshifting to reduce speed should only supplement the brakes [A01].
Why it matters: the missing stop-lamp warning is the reason the manual discourages habitual downshifting.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec14-F03 | anchor: A01
At normal highway speeds every passenger car automatic transmission downshifts by itself when the accelerator is fully depressed, downshifting at higher speeds may actually reduce the vehicle's ability to accelerate, and abusing the technique stresses the engine and transmission and can lead to costly repairs [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec14-F04 | anchor: A01
Downshifting is a proper emergency procedure for slowing a vehicle after partial or complete brake failure, but it needs extra care on a slippery surface because the unequal forces it creates can cause control problems [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec14-F05 | anchor: A01
Always park where the vehicle is clear of traffic and readily visible to approaching drivers, avoiding hidden spots such as just beyond a curve or the crest of a hill [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec14-F06 | anchor: A01
When parking on a hill, always set the hand brake, shift to park if the vehicle has it or otherwise into reverse or low gear, and turn the front wheels toward the curb so that all four wheels would have to climb the curb before the vehicle could roll free [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec14-F07 | anchor: A01
Whether you park uphill or downhill, the manual directs you to turn the wheels to the right so that a vehicle that rolls free rolls away from traffic [A01].
Why it matters: this manual's hill rule is turn right either way, which differs from the uphill-versus-downhill rule many learners expect.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec14-F08 | anchor: A02
For angle parking, keep safe clearance and drive forward into the space with equal room on each side between the lines [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec14-F09 | anchor: A02
Parallel parking begins by signaling and stopping even with the front car about eighteen inches from it with the rear bumpers even, then backing slowly with the wheel turned sharply right until the car is at about a forty-five degree angle to the street, then quickly straightening the front wheels and backing slowly [A02].
Why it matters: eighteen inches and forty-five degrees are the two numbers of the first two steps.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec14-F10 | anchor: A02
When your front bumper is even with the other car's rear bumper, turn the wheel sharply and rapidly all the way left and back slowly toward the car behind without touching it, then turn sharply right, pull forward slowly and center the car in the space [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec14-F11 | anchor: A02
When parallel parked, your front and rear bumpers should be no closer than two feet to the other vehicles unless the street is marked otherwise [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec14-F12 | anchor: A03
Unless angle parking is clearly designated, you park parallel to the curb facing the direction of traffic, with the curbside wheels no more than twelve inches from the curb or the whole vehicle inside the marked stall [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec14-F13 | anchor: A03
Electric stop signals have been standard for more than fifty years, most vehicles built since the early nineteen fifties have electric turn signals, and since nineteen sixty-eight every vehicle has had electric turn, stop and four-way hazard signals [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec14-F14 | anchor: A03
Electric signals can be operated instantly from a closed vehicle, are visible in darkness and bad weather and from all angles except the immediate sides, are seldom misinterpreted, and leave both hands free for control [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec14-F15 | anchor: A03
The disadvantages of electric signals are failure to cancel and failure to function, and a failure to cancel usually comes from a turn or lane change too small to trip the self-cancelling mechanism combined with the driver not watching the panel indicator, whose abnormal behavior is the clue to a signal problem [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec14-F16 | anchor: A03
Hand signals remain an accepted way to show intentions and knowing them is required in case the electric signals fail, their only advantage being that they are seldom subject to failure [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec14-F17 | anchor: A03
Hand signals are hard to tell from other arm motions, hard to see in darkness and bad weather, not readily visible to drivers on the right, require an open window, and leave only one hand on the wheel [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec14-F18 | anchor: A03
The four-way hazard flashers tell other drivers that your vehicle is stopped in a hazardous spot on the roadway; they must never be used while moving, they show as every turn indicator flashing, and no hand signal exists for them [A03].
Why it matters: never while moving, and no hand signal exists for it.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec14-F19 | anchor: A04
Electric stop lamps operate automatically when the service brake is used, at night their glow should be visible behind the vehicle when you press the pedal, and a hand signal may be used to show braking or slowing [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec14-F20 | anchor: A04
A turn signal shows your intent but gives you no right to make the move, you alone are responsible for making it safely, and traffic regulations require the signal for at least one hundred feet before every turn or lane change and long enough for others to see and understand it [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec14-F21 | anchor: A04
If you must slow before a turn or lane change, begin signaling before you slow so other drivers are alerted that you may reduce speed [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec14-F22 | anchor: A04
Common signaling errors are waiting at a red light without signaling the intended turn, signaling too briefly or only after the move has begun, not signaling a right turn, not signaling in a lane that requires a turn, and not signaling because no one seems to be watching [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec14-F23 | anchor: A04
Failing to signal properly is a frequent driver error that shows ignorance, arrogance or uncertainty and a lack of courtesy, and it may mean the driver has no idea what to do next [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec14-F24 | anchor: A04
The three rules of turn signals are to signal every time you intend to turn or change lanes, to begin well in advance so others can see and understand, and to remember that the signal shows intent only and grants no right to move [A04].
Why it matters: the three capitalized rules are the manual's summary and a natural list question.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec14-F25 | anchor: A04
You share the road with trucks, buses, cars, motorcycles, bicycles and pedestrians, and larger vehicles protect their occupants more and are easier to see but harder to operate, while small vehicles protect less and are less visible but more agile [A04].
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec14-F26 | anchor: A05
Recognize the capabilities and limits of other vehicles and your own, look carefully for smaller vehicles such as motorcycles and bicycles, and make sure the drivers of trucks and buses can see you [A05].
Source: [A05 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0075]

FACT_ID: sec14-F27 | anchor: A05
Give motorcyclists, bicyclists and pedestrians plenty of room and look for them with extra care when turning or changing lanes, and a motorcyclist is entitled to the entire width of the traffic lane [A05].
Source: [A05 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0075]

FACT_ID: sec14-F28 | anchor: A05
Hawaii's weather problems for drivers come mainly from rain, with isolated fog on high-elevation roads and occasional gusty winds, and rain both reduces visibility and changes the road surface [A05].
Source: [A05 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0075]

FACT_ID: sec14-F29 | anchor: A05
The first few drops of rain are a danger signal, because the road is most slippery before the oil dropped by passing cars has washed away and oil on water can feel like ice, so slow down, add caution and keep at least double your usual following distance [A05].
Why it matters: twice the normal following distance is the rain rule.
Source: [A05 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0075]

FACT_ID: sec14-F30 | anchor: A05
Prolonged or heavy rain leaves a layer of water on the road, and at speeds up to thirty-five miles per hour tires with good highway tread wipe the surface like a windshield wiper, but at higher speeds the water cannot be cleared and the tires ride up on it like a surfboard, which is called hydroplaning [A05].
Source: [A05 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0075]

FACT_ID: sec14-F31 | anchor: A05
Partial hydroplaning may begin at thirty-five miles per hour, it grows with speed and with the amount of water, and at fifty-five miles per hour in heavy rain the tires may lose all contact with the pavement, leaving you unable to brake, accelerate or steer [A05].
Why it matters: thirty-five starts it and fifty-five can mean total loss of contact.
Source: [A05 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0075]

FACT_ID: sec14-F32 | anchor: A06
To prevent hydroplaning keep good tread depth, because worn or bald tires hydroplane at lower speeds, keep tires at proper pressure, because under-inflated tires hydroplane at lower speeds, and reduce speed, because hydroplaning happens most at higher speeds [A06].
Source: [A06 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0076]

FACT_ID: sec14-F33 | anchor: A06
After deep water or prolonged heavy rain the brakes may be wet and pull to one side or not hold at all, so reduce speed and apply gentle pedal pressure until they work properly again [A06].
Source: [A06 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0076]

FACT_ID: sec14-F34 | anchor: A06
When heavy rain cuts visibility even with the wipers running, reduce speed and turn on the low-beam head lamps so others can see you, and if you still cannot see clearly, pull onto the shoulder or another clear area and stop until the rain lets up [A06].
Source: [A06 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0076]

FACT_ID: sec14-F35 | anchor: A06
Avoid driving through flooded areas because you may be stranded, and never drive through swiftly moving water more than one foot deep, which will sweep the vehicle off the road [A06].
Source: [A06 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0076]

FACT_ID: sec14-F36 | anchor: A06
Fog in Hawaii almost never occurs at low elevations but can meet the road at higher elevations where low clouds touch the ground, and patches of fog are especially hazardous because they appear suddenly [A06].
Source: [A06 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0076]

FACT_ID: sec14-F37 | anchor: A06
In fog, sharply reduce speed and use low beams, never high beams, whose reflection reduces your own vision and the approaching driver's, be ready for an emergency stop, and if you cannot see at least two car lengths, about forty feet, pull completely off the pavement, stop and turn on the hazard signals [A06].
Why it matters: two car lengths or forty feet is the stop threshold, and these fog rules apply whenever visibility is reduced for any reason.
Source: [A06 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0076]

FACT_ID: sec14-F38 | anchor: A06
Winter driving elsewhere brings hazards unknown in Hawaii, and unless experienced you should avoid it, otherwise fit snow tread tires, start slowly and test the brakes gently once moving, keep the windows clear of snow, ice and frost, keep a safe distance and watch for vehicles in trouble, drive slower and stay on the clear dry parts of the road [A06].
Source: [A06 -> src:rdmv-hi-x:hawaii-department-of-transportation-hdot:handbook:pdf-0076]

Misconceptions: hazard flashers are never used while moving; the first drops of rain make the road most slippery, not a long downpour; in fog you use low beams, never high beams; hydroplaning can begin at thirty-five miles per hour, not only at freeway speed; this manual says to turn the wheels to the right on a hill whether parked uphill or downhill; a signal is required even in a lane that forces a turn and even when no one seems to be watching; routine downshifting is discouraged because it gives no stop-lamp warning.

Mnemonics: Twice the distance when rain begins, thirty-five starts hydroplaning and fifty-five can float the tires; low beams in fog and rain, stop at two car lengths; eighteen inches and forty-five degrees to parallel park, two feet to each neighbor, twelve inches to the curb; wheels right on a hill.

Glossary: hydroplaning (tires riding on a film of water with no pavement contact); hazard warning signal (the four-way flash used only when stopped in a hazardous position); self-cancelling mechanism (the device that turns a signal off after a turn); traffic mix (the range of vehicle sizes sharing the road); curbside wheels (the wheels nearest the curb when parallel parked).

Dynamic facts: none; the weather rules, signal law and parking rules are stable content of this printing, and the signal history dates are stated only as printed.
